posts.title: Best Tech Stack for Your Startup Website: MERN vs Next.js vs WordPress
posts.excerpt: Not sure whether to build your startup website with MERN, Next.js or WordPress? Compare cost, speed, scalability and SEO to pick the right stack.
posts.author: Borhan U.

content.text: Once a startup decides to enter the market, one of the first big questions is how to build its digital footprint. Your website is your shop window, your sales agent and often your first impression. Choose the wrong technology and you may pay for it later with slow pages, high maintenance bills or a painful rebuild.
If you are asking what the best tech stack for a startup website is, this guide will help you decide. We compare MERN, Next.js and WordPress in plain language so you can choose with confidence.
Quick overview of the three options

items: MERN stands for MongoDB, Express.js, React and Node.js. It is a full JavaScript stack that gives you complete control over the frontend and the backend, which makes it ideal for custom web applications.
Next.js is a React framework that supports server side rendering and static generation. It is known for speed, strong SEO and flexibility, and it suits marketing sites and full applications alike.
WordPress is a content management system that powers a huge share of the web. It is fast to launch, easy to manage and backed by thousands of themes and plugins.

content.text: Four questions to ask before you choose

items: What is your business for and how big is it?
What type of content will your site have?
How many users may visit?
How much are you willing to invest?

content.text: 1. Your business type and size

Imagine you run a consultancy in your local area and most of your work happens offline. You need a clean website that explains your services, builds trust and brings in enquiries. WordPress is usually the most practical choice here because it is quick to launch, cheap to run and easy for a non technical team to update. A Next.js marketing site is a great option too if you want top speed and a more custom design.

Now imagine a large shop or retail company that needs an ecommerce website where customers browse, pay, track orders and manage accounts. WordPress with WooCommerce works well for small and medium stores. For a large catalogue, custom pricing rules, multi vendor features or complex integrations, Next.js with a custom backend or a MERN application gives you far more control and room to grow.

items: Small business with mostly informational needs: WordPress or Next.js
Growing online business with custom features: Next.js
Software product, marketplace or platform: MERN or Next.js with a Node backend

content.text: 2. What types of content will your site have?

Static content such as Home, About, Services and Contact pages rarely changes. WordPress and Next.js both handle this very well. Next.js can pre-build these pages, which makes them load extremely fast and helps your Google rankings.

If your team publishes blog posts often, WordPress has the friendliest editor and the best out of the box SEO tools. Next.js can do the same when paired with a headless CMS, though it needs more setup.

Highly dynamic content such as dashboards, user accounts, live data, chat, bookings and personalised feeds needs a proper application. This is where MERN and Next.js shine. WordPress can stretch to cover some of it with plugins, but too many plugins slow your site and increase security risk.
3. How many users may visit?
Traffic matters because the stack you pick decides how easily you can grow.

items: WordPress handles low to medium traffic well. At higher traffic it needs caching, a CDN, optimised hosting and careful plugin management. It can scale, but it takes effort and budget.
Next.js is excellent for scale. Static pages can be served from a CDN around the world, which keeps your site fast even when traffic spikes.

MERN uses Node.js to handle many concurrent connections efficiently and MongoDB to scale horizontally. It suits applications with many active users, provided the architecture is designed well from day one.

content.text: In short, Next.js usually leads for the balance of speed, SEO and scalability. MERN is a proven choice for heavy application workloads. WordPress is perfectly fine for small to medium traffic.
4. How much are you willing to invest?
Your cost is more than the build. Think about hosting, a domain, security, updates, backups and ongoing maintenance. Real costs vary by project, so treat the levels below as general guidance.

items: Low budget: WordPress on shared hosting or cPanel with premium themes and plugins. Delivery is quick, but you must watch plugin updates, security patches and vulnerability risks.
Medium budget: Next.js in static or hybrid mode on modern hosting or a small VPS. You get a custom design with better speed and SEO, but you need a developer for changes.
High budget: MERN or a full custom Next.js build on cloud infrastructure with databases, APIs, monitoring, DevOps and regular developer support. The cost is higher and so is the control.

content.text: Hidden costs to remember:

items: WordPress: premium plugin licences, security tools, frequent updates and cleanup after hacks
Next.js and MERN: developer time, cloud and database costs and monitoring
All stacks: backups, SSL, uptime monitoring and performance tuning

content.text: Which stack for which type of website?

items: Company portfolio: WordPress or Next.js. WordPress is the cheapest and fastest to launch while Next.js gives better performance and a more unique design.

Ecommerce store: WordPress with WooCommerce for small stores, Next.js with a headless commerce backend for growing brands and MERN for custom marketplaces. Speed directly affects sales, so performance matters here.

LMS: MERN or Next.js with a Node backend for a custom platform with user roles, video, quizzes, progress tracking and payments. WordPress with an LMS plugin works for a simple course site with a small student base.
Real estate website: Next.js. Property listings need fast search, filters, maps and strong SEO for local keywords. WordPress can work for a small agency with few listings.
SaaS or web application: MERN or Next.js. You need custom logic, authentication, dashboards and APIs, which these stacks are built for.

content.text: Frequently asked questions

items: Is WordPress good for startups? Yes, when you need to launch quickly on a limited budget. It becomes harder to manage when you need heavy customisation or high performance at scale.

Is Next.js better than WordPress for SEO? Next.js can deliver faster pages and cleaner code, which supports better Core Web Vitals. WordPress has excellent SEO plugins and is easy to optimise. Both can rank very well when set up properly.
Is MERN good for a startup website? It is great for web apps and platforms. For a simple marketing site it is often more than you need.
Can I switch from WordPress to Next.js later? Yes. Many businesses start with WordPress and migrate later. Planning for it early saves time and money.

content.text: Our final advice

There is no single best stack for every startup. Choose WordPress when you need speed to market and a low budget. Choose Next.js when performance, SEO and scalability matter most. Choose MERN when you are building a custom platform or application. The smartest approach is to match the technology to your business goals today while leaving room for growth tomorrow.

posts.title: Website Security Testing: Risks, Process and Checklist
posts.excerpt: Learn how website security testing uncovers hidden vulnerabilities, what a penetration test includes, and when to assess your business website.
posts.author: OrbitWick Team

content.text: Your website loads quickly, forms work correctly and customers can complete purchases. But a website that works as expected can still contain security weaknesses. Website security testing examines whether your application protects its data, accounts and business functions when someone interacts with it in unexpected ways.

For businesses, these weaknesses can affect customer trust, service availability and the confidentiality of sensitive information. Understanding what to test helps you make security part of your website's development and maintenance.
What is website security testing?

Website security testing is the assessment of a website and its supporting application components to identify vulnerabilities. Depending on the agreed scope, it can cover login systems, access permissions, forms, file uploads, sessions, APIs and deployment settings.

The aim is to identify weaknesses, establish their potential impact and provide practical recommendations. A useful assessment explains what needs fixing, why it matters and how to verify the improvement.
Functional testing vs security testing

Functional testing checks whether features behave as intended. Security testing examines whether those features can be misused or accessed without the correct permissions. Both are necessary, but they answer different questions.

items: A functional test checks whether a customer can view an order. A security test checks whether they can access another customer's order.
A functional test checks whether a password reset email arrives. A security test examines whether the reset process protects the account.
A functional test checks whether a file uploads successfully. A security test examines whether the application rejects unsafe files and controls access to stored uploads.

content.text: Common website security risks
Security weaknesses can exist in application code, configuration and business workflows. The following areas deserve attention during a web application security assessment.

items: Broken access control: Users can view data or perform actions outside their permitted role.
Authentication and session weaknesses: Login, password recovery or session handling fails to protect user accounts adequately.
Injection vulnerabilities: Untrusted input changes how a backend command or query is interpreted.
Cross-site scripting: Unsafe handling of content allows unwanted scripts to run in a visitor's browser.
Unsafe file uploads: Uploaded files are insufficiently validated, stored or served.
Security misconfiguration: Debug information, unnecessary services or inappropriate settings expose the application.
Vulnerable dependencies: Outdated components introduce known weaknesses.
Business logic flaws: Application workflows allow actions that violate intended business rules.

content.text: Vulnerability assessment vs penetration testing

A vulnerability assessment identifies and prioritizes potential weaknesses. Penetration testing goes further by attempting to validate exploitable weaknesses within an agreed scope and demonstrate their impact. The activities can overlap, so the deliverables should be defined before testing starts.

Automated scanning can support both approaches, but it does not replace examination of application-specific permissions and workflows. A scanner may detect a suspicious configuration without understanding how a customer account or approval process should behave.
What does a website security assessment include?

items: Scope agreement: Define the website, environments, accounts, integrations and testing limits.
Application review: Understand important features, user roles and sensitive data flows.
Security testing: Assess relevant authentication, authorization, input handling, session management and configuration controls.
Finding validation: Confirm suspected weaknesses and record supporting evidence.
Risk prioritization: Explain the likely impact and conditions required for exploitation.
Remediation guidance: Recommend practical changes for the development or operations team.
Retesting: Check whether the implemented fixes address the reported issues.

content.text: Website security checklist for businesses

items: Keep application frameworks, plugins and dependencies updated.
Use HTTPS and protect sensitive configuration and credentials.
Apply appropriate access permissions to customer, staff and administrator accounts.
Use multi-factor authentication where supported, particularly for privileged accounts.
Validate input and handle output safely.
Review file upload restrictions and storage permissions.
Protect login, password recovery and session workflows.
Maintain backups and test the recovery process.
Monitor relevant security events without unnecessarily recording sensitive data.
Review security after significant changes and verify important fixes.

content.text: When should you test your website?

Consider an assessment before launching a new website, after a major redesign or migration, and when introducing sensitive features such as payments, customer accounts or administrative tools. Changes to permissions and integrations also deserve review.

The frequency of ongoing testing should reflect the sensitivity of your data, how often the application changes and the risks your business faces. An assessment captures conditions at a particular time; ongoing maintenance remains necessary.
Does HTTPS mean a website is secure?

HTTPS protects data in transit between a visitor and the server. It does not establish that the application has correct access controls, safe input handling or secure business workflows. A website needs protection at several layers.
Can security testing guarantee that a website is safe?

No assessment can guarantee the absence of vulnerabilities. Testing helps uncover weaknesses within the agreed scope and time available. Its value comes from addressing the findings and maintaining security as the application evolves.

posts.title: API Security Testing: Common Risks and a Practical Checklist
posts.excerpt: Explore common API security risks, how an assessment works, and practical checks for authentication, access control, sensitive data and rate limits.
posts.author: OrbitWick Team

content.text: APIs connect websites, mobile applications and business systems. They exchange data, support account access and enable transactions. API security testing examines whether these interfaces protect information and enforce the rules that determine who can access each resource or action.

An application can appear secure while its API exposes sensitive information or permits unauthorized actions. Testing the interface directly helps identify weaknesses that may not be visible through the website or mobile app.
What is API security testing?

API security testing evaluates an API's authentication, authorization, data handling and resistance to misuse. An assessment examines requests and responses alongside the application's intended permissions and business rules.
A useful assessment does more than list suspicious endpoints. It validates findings, explains their potential impact and gives developers practical guidance for remediation.
Why APIs need dedicated security testing

APIs expose application functions directly to clients. Restrictions in a website interface do not necessarily prevent a user from sending a request to the underlying API. Security controls must therefore be enforced by the server.

items: Web and mobile clients may share endpoints that return sensitive information.
Different roles may require different permissions for the same resource.
Older API versions can remain accessible after a replacement is released.
Resource-intensive operations can create availability and cost risks.
Changes to an endpoint can affect several connected applications.

content.text: Common API security vulnerabilities
The following examples are useful assessment areas rather than an exhaustive list. Their relevance depends on the API's architecture, data and business functions.

items: Broken object-level authorization: Access to an individual record is not checked correctly.
Broken authentication: Identity verification or token handling can be bypassed or misused.
Broken property-level authorization: Users can read or modify fields beyond their permissions.
Broken function-level authorization: Restricted actions are available to unauthorized roles.
Unrestricted resource consumption: Requests can consume excessive computing or paid service resources.
Security misconfiguration: Inappropriate settings weaken protection or expose unnecessary information.
Improper inventory management: Older or undocumented endpoints escape security oversight.

content.text: Authentication vs authorization in APIs

Authentication establishes who is making a request. Authorization determines what that identity may access or change. A successful login does not give a user permission to view every record or invoke every operation.

For example, an API serving customer invoices must check access to the requested invoice, not simply confirm that the caller is signed in. Using identifiers that are difficult to guess does not replace a permission check.
Protecting sensitive API response data
An API should return only the information the caller needs and is permitted to receive. Internal account attributes, confidential business fields and privileged settings require explicit controls.

Write operations need the same care. Developers should define which properties a caller may change instead of accepting every field included in a request. These rules should reflect both the user's role and the current business context.
Why rate limits are only part of API protection

Limiting request frequency helps control abuse, but individual requests can also be expensive. Large uploads, broad searches and complex reports may consume substantial resources even at a low request rate.

Review request sizes, pagination, timeouts, concurrency and usage quotas as appropriate. Controls should reflect the cost and purpose of the operation rather than applying one limit to every endpoint.
Automated scanning vs manual API testing

Automated tools help discover endpoints and flag some configuration or input-handling issues. They are useful for repeatable checks, but they may not understand the permissions and business rules specific to your application.

Manual assessment examines those relationships. It can compare permitted behavior across accounts and roles, evaluate multi-step workflows and determine whether a suspected weakness has a meaningful impact. Combining both approaches provides broader coverage.
What happens during an API security assessment?

items: Define the scope: Agree on API hosts, environments, endpoints, accounts and operational limits.
Review the interface: Examine documentation, request formats, supported versions and important workflows.
Assess authentication: Review credential handling, token validation and relevant session controls.
Assess authorization: Check permissions across users, roles, resources, properties and operations.
Review data handling: Examine input validation, error responses and sensitive information exposure.
Evaluate resource controls: Review limits on requests and expensive operations within the agreed scope.
Validate findings: Confirm issues with controlled testing and document supporting evidence.
Provide remediation guidance: Explain affected components, impact, priorities and recommended changes.
Retest fixes: Verify that reported weaknesses have been addressed.

content.text: API security checklist for development teams

items: Require appropriate authentication for protected endpoints.
Enforce server-side permissions for sensitive records, fields and actions.
Validate request parameters, content types and input data.
Return only the information each caller is permitted to receive.
Apply suitable request limits, quotas and resource controls.
Protect credentials, tokens, secrets and configuration.
Use HTTPS to protect data in transit.
Avoid exposing sensitive information in errors or logs.
Maintain an inventory of API versions, endpoints and owners.
Retire obsolete endpoints and review access to non-production environments.
Review permissions when roles or business workflows change.
Include relevant security checks in release workflows and retest significant fixes.

content.text: When should you test your APIs?

Assess APIs before launching sensitive functionality and after significant changes to authentication, permissions or business workflows. New integrations, mobile applications and administrative features can also introduce risks that deserve review.

Ongoing assessment frequency should reflect how often the API changes, what data it handles and its importance to business operations. Keep documentation and endpoint inventories current between assessments.
Do private APIs need security testing?

Yes. Restricting network access can reduce exposure, but it does not establish that permissions and data handling are correct. Internal applications, integrations and compromised accounts may still interact with a private API.
What should an API security report include?

A useful report identifies the assessment scope, affected endpoints, validated findings, supporting evidence and potential impact. It should explain remediation priorities and distinguish confirmed vulnerabilities from observations or testing limitations.
